ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the institutional Ethics Review Board (Approval No.
I-19-96) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Between April and December 2021, 56 patients hospitalized for acute HF (mean age 74 years, 35% women, 46% HFrEF) were enrolled from 176 screened patients at a single center.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment.
This report presents findings from participants enrolled between April and December 2021 with one-year follow-up thereafter.
Participants were asked about their routines for using the handbook, the perceived benefits and challenges, and how discharge education shaped their self-management practices at home.

ethics_check.report:

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: Heart failure knowledge test scores at baseline, prior to nurse-led education, were similar between groups (median [IQR]: 10 [6-13] in the improved group and 10 [8-13] in the non-improved group; P = 0.95).

table.header: Heart failure knowledge at pre, post education, and initial outpatient visit
table.expanded: Similarly, at the initial outpatient visit, knowledge scores remained higher in the improved group (16 [12-18]) than in the non-improved group (13 [10-16]; P = 0.021).

table.header: Heart failure knowledge at pre, post education, and initial outpatient visit
table.expanded: The largest difference was observed for the item "It is better to avoid exercise as much as possible" (Q8), which was correctly answered by 83.9% (26/31) of patients in the knowledge improved group compared with 40.0% (8/25) in the non improved group (difference 43.9%, P = 0.001).

table.formatted: Similarly, the item "Heart failure may cause frequent urination at night" (Q7) showed correct response rates of 93.5% (29/31) versus 50.0% (10/25), respectively (difference 43.5%, P < 0.001).

table.header: Heart failure knowledge at pre, post education, and initial outpatient visit
table.expanded: A large difference was also observed for the question "One pickled plum (10 g) contains 0.5 g of salt" (Q10), with correct responses in 77.4% (24/31) of the knowledge improved group and 35.0% (7/25) of the non improved group (difference 42.4%, P = 0.002).

table.header: Heart failure knowledge at pre, post education, and initial outpatient visit
table.expanded: In addition, for the item "Even mild diarrhea can worsen heart failure" (Q14), correct response rates were 73.3% (22/31) in the knowledge improved group and 31.6% (6/25) in the non improved group (difference 41.7%, P = 0.004).

Heart failure handbook diary completion for recording vital signs, body weight, and symptoms was similar across groups (41 [73%] overall; 23 [74%] in the improved group; 18 [72%] in the nonimproved group; P = 0.29).

The change in KCCQ-12 Score from pre-education to the initial outpatient visit was similar between groups (median [IQR]: 19 [-5 to 42] in the improved group vs. 14 [-6 to 41] in the non-improved group; P = 0.86).

table.formatted: The proportion of patients achieving a clinically meaningful improvement in KCCQ-12 Score(>5-point increase) was similar between groups (overall: 21 [64%]; improved group: 13 [68%]; non-improved group: 8 [57%]; P = 0.72).
table.expanded: The proportion of patients achieving a clinically meaningful improvement in KCCQ-12 Score(>5-point increase) was similar between groups (overall: 21 [64%]; improved group: 13 [68%]; non-improved group: 8 [57%]; P = 0.72).
All-cause mortality occurred in 3 of 28 patients (10.7%) in the knowledge-improved group and in 1 of 23 patients (4.3%) in the non-improved group (P = 0.40).
Heart failure-related readmission occurred in 5 of 28 patients (17.9%) in the knowledge-improved group and in 3 of 23 patients (13.0%) in the non-improved group (P = 0.64).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.38", "P = 0.95", "P = 0.29", "P = 0.86", "P = 0.72", "P = 0.40", "P = 0.64"), Sentence = c("39 [29-57] ; P = 0.38).", "Heart failure knowledge test scores at baseline, prior to nurse-led education, were similar between groups (median [IQR]: 10 [6-13] in the improved group and 10 [8-13] in the non-improved group; P = 0.95).", "Heart failure handbook diary completion for recording vital signs, body weight, and symptoms was similar across groups (41 [73%] overall; 23 [74%] in the improved group; 18 [72%] in the nonimproved group; P = 0.29).", "The change in KCCQ-12 Score from pre-education to the initial outpatient visit was similar between groups (median [IQR]: 19 [-5 to 42] in the improved group vs. 14 [-6 to 41] in the non-improved group; P = 0.86).", "The proportion of patients achieving a clinically meaningful improvement in KCCQ-12 Score(>5-point increase) was similar between groups (overall: 21 [64%]; improved group: 13 [68%]; non-improved group: 8 [57%]; P = 0.72).", "All-cause mortality occurred in 3 of 28 patients (10.7%) in the knowledge-improved group and in 1 of 23 patients (4.3%) in the non-improved group (P = 0.40).", "Heart failure-related readmission occurred in 5 of 28 patients (17.9%) in the knowledge-improved group and in 3 of 23 patients (13.0%) in the non-improved group (P = 0.64)." )), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
